{{short description|American economist and statistician}}
'''Ida Craven Merriam''' (1904–1997)<ref>Birth date from {{harvtxt|Estes|2013}}; the listing in ''Social Security Pioneers'' gives her birthdate as 1905.</ref> was an American [[economist]] and [[statistician]] who became "one of the seminal figures in the early administration of the [[Social Security (United States)|Social Security]] program",<ref name="pioneers">{{citation|url=https://www.ssa.gov/history/idamer.html|title=Ida Craven Merriam|work=Social Security Pioneers|publisher=Social Security Administration|accessdate=2016-07-21}}</ref> helping to found the nonprofit National Academy of Social Insurance.<ref name="siu"/><ref name="estes">{{citation|last=Estes|first=R.J.|date=April 2013|doi=10.1007/s11482-013-9227-9|issue=2|journal=Applied Research in Quality of Life|pages=275–76|title=Ida Craven Merriam (1904–1997): A leading figure in Social Security and quality of life research|volume=8|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Ida Craven, a native of [[Philadelphia, Pennsylvania]], was born on November 6, 1904.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.fold3.com/record/79584549-ida-c-merriam?terms=Merriam|title=Ida C Merriam|accessdate=August 1, 2020}}</ref> She graduated [[Phi Beta Kappa]] in English and history from [[Wellesley College]] in 1925,<ref name="pioneers"/><ref name="wp"/><ref name="estes"/> where she was president of the Wellesley Forum.<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.thecrimson.com/article/1924/9/29/wellesley-politicians-ask-harvard-men-to|title=Wellesley Politicians Ask Harvard Men To Speak|newspaper=[[The Harvard Crimson]]|date=September 29, 1924}}.</ref> She studied economics at the [[University of Chicago]], and then earned a Ph.D. in 1928 from the [[Brookings Institution|Brookings Graduate School of Economics and Government]] in [[Washington, D.C.]]<ref name="pioneers"/><ref name="wp"/><ref name="estes"/> While working towards her doctorate at Brookings, she taught a summer economics class at the [[Bryn Mawr Summer School for Women Workers in Industry]].<ref>{{citation|title=College Notes|page=5|newspaper=Wellesley College News|date=September 29, 1927|url=http://repository.wellesley.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1766&context=news|access-date=July 21, 2016|archive-date=September 21, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160921221014/http://repository.wellesley.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1766&context=news|url-status=dead}}.</ref> After completing her studies, she worked for the ''Encyclopedia of Social Sciences'' and as an assistant professor at the [[Connecticut College|Connecticut College for Women]], and married Mylon Merriam in 1933.<ref name="wp"/>

She left her position at Connecticut College in 1936 to work in the research and statistics bureau of the Social Security Administration,<ref name="pioneers"/><ref>{{citation|title=Mrs. Ida Merriam Takes Federal Post In Washington, D.C.|newspaper=Connecticut College News|date=May 30, 1936|volume=21|issue=25|url=http://digitalcommons.conncoll.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1024&context=ccnews_1935_1936|page=4}}.</ref> soon after the creation of the SSA in 1935,<ref name="estes"/> She became the head of that unit<ref name="pioneers"/> and Assistant Commissioner of the Office of Research and Statistics in 1955.<ref name="wp">{{citation|title=Ida Merriam Dies at 92|newspaper=[[Washington Post]]|date=April 9, 1997|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1997/04/09/ida-merriam-dies-at-92/44f93fd7-0e80-4153-bcb2-9c4c11bec8c5}}{{subscription required}}</ref> As Assistant Commissioner, she published special reports on topics including housing, benefit levels, health insurance, disability, widows, work-life balance, prospects for future retirees, and related social welfare systems in Europe. Her unit also set the first [[poverty threshold]]s for the US.<ref name="siu">{{citation|title=Ida C. Merriam|journal=Social Insurance Update|volume=1|issue=2|date=March 1996|pages=9–10|publisher=National Academy of Social Insurance|url=https://www.ssa.gov/history/idanasi.html}}.</ref> She retired in 1972.<ref name="pioneers"/>

In 1965, she was elected as a [[Fellow]] of the [[American Statistical Association]] "for outstanding sustained accomplishments and contributions through statistical research to social insurance and social welfare."<ref>{{citation|year=1965|title=New ASA Fellows—1965|journal=[[The American Statistician]]|volume=19|issue=4|pages=37–38|doi=10.1080/00031305.1965.10479746}}.</ref> The [[United States Civil Service Commission]] gave Merriam a Federal Woman's Award in 1966, and she also won the Distinguished Service Award of the [[Department of Health, Education and Welfare]].<ref name="wp"/><ref name="estes"/>

==Death==
Ida Craven Merriam died on April 8, 1997, in [[Cheverly, Maryland]], near the Collington Episcopal Life Care Center in [[Mitchellville, Maryland]], where she had been an inpatient for three years before her death.<ref name="wp"/>
